newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq says "oil-for-food" deal can now go ahead.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says "oil-for-food" deal can now go ahead.

text.p: Iraqi U.N. Ambassador Nizar Hamdoon said on Monday Baghdad had agreed to all U.N. conditions that had held up implementation of an "oil-for-food" deal and predicted oil could start flowing in December.

He was speaking to reporters after a meeting with Undersecretary-General Chinmaya Gharekhan, who heads a U.N. task force overseeing the deal, which would permit the sale of $2 billion of Iraqi oil over six months, on a renewable basis.
One remaining step is for the Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee to approve an oil pricing formula governing future oil contracts.
Iraq last week submitted a formula for December to U.N. oil overseers who were to pass it on to the sanctions committee later on Monday with their observations.
The United States delayed committee approval of formulas for previous months, saying other problems must first be worked out.
Asked about prospects for approval now, in light of Iraq's acceptance of U.N. terms, deputy United States U.N. representative Edward Gnhem told Reuters: "I don't think there will be a problem."
"We have always said that when there was a realistic probability that there would be implementation (of the deal) that we didn't have a problem in principle with the oil pricing formula," he said.

U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa confirmed that "Iraq agrees with the views of the U.N. secretariat on the modalities of implementation" of the oil deal and quoted Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali as saying: "I am optimistic we will have movement within the next few weeks."

She said the United Nations would have to send experts back to northern Iraq to check that oil metering equipment on the Iraq-Turkish border, which had not been in working order, was functioning properly. The bulk of the Iraqi oil was due to flow through a pipeline to Turkey, with the remainder being exported via the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr.

The "oil-for-food" deal concluded between Iraq and the United Nations in May but delayed due to differences over how it should be carried out, was to help ease the effects on ordinary Iraqis of crippling economic sanctions imposed soon after President Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
One of the obstacles has been Iraqi insistence on controlling the number, make-up and freedom of movement of U.N. observers who would monitor arrangements on the ground.
"All the aspects of the MOU (memorandum of understanding signed in May) have been discussed and they have been agreed upon," Hamdoon said, including the issue of U.N. observers.
Asked when Iraqi oil might begin to flow, he said: "December, I think, is the most likely time for the oil to start moving, because there is nothing else to impede the process.

"I met Mr. Gharekhan and told him Iraq has agreed to implement the memorandum of understanding according to the modalities that were discussed between both sides in the last, I would say, couple of months ... so Iraq now is ready for the smooth and easy implementation of the MOU," Hamdoon said, adding that he gave Gharekhan a letter setting out "the official Iraqi acceptance" of the terms for the deal.
Hamdoon said the pipeline to Turkey "will definitely be ready by the first week of December."
"If the pricing formula is approved -- which we hope to get this week -- then nothing else remains," he said, alluding to action by the sanctions committee.
